articles.title: Bioengineered gum could expand treatment options for oral cancer patients
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A bioengineered chewing gum cut HPV levels by 93 percent in oral samples from head and neck cancer patients, in new research from the University of Pennsylvania. The same formulation, when loaded with an antimicrobial peptide called protegrin, brought two cancer-linked bacteria down to nearly zero and left the […]
The post Bioengineered gum could expand treatment options for oral cancer patients first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

A bioengineered chewing gum cut HPV levels by 93 percent in oral samples from head and neck cancer patients, in new research from the University of Pennsylvania. The same formulation, when loaded with an antimicrobial peptide called protegrin, brought two cancer-linked bacteria down to nearly zero and left the mouth’s beneficial microbes alone.

Henry Daniell of Penn’s School of Dental Medicine led the work, published in Scientific Reports.

Why head and neck cancer needs new treatment options

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, or HNSCC, starts in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It’s often caught late, and newer drugs haven’t done much to improve survival rates. That’s pushed researchers toward other angles.

HPV sits at the center of the problem. “The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection,” says Daniell. Two bacteria make outcomes worse: Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum. “Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies.”

How does the gum work?

The gum is made from lablab beans, which naturally contain FRIL, an antiviral protein. Daniell’s team tested extracts against oral samples from HNSCC patients. HPV dropped by 93 percent in saliva and 80 percent in oral rinse samples.

For the bacteria, the team added protegrin to the formulation. A single dose brought both Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum to nearly nothing.

A treatment that leaves the microbiome intact

The part worth paying attention to is what the gum didn’t do. Radiation therapy, standard in head and neck cancer treatment, tends to knock out helpful bacteria while creating conditions that favor Candida albicans, a disease-causing yeast. The bean gum avoided that collateral damage, which matters because it could run alongside existing treatments without making the microbial picture worse.

The case for clinical trials

Daniell puts the scale of the problem plainly: “Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022. Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission.”

The team sees two applications: as an add-on to existing cancer treatment, and as a preventive against HPV transmission. These results come from lab tests on patient samples. Clinical trials are the next step.

Source study: Scientific Reports– Ex vivo HNSCC clinical studies using saliva and antiviral or antibacterial chewing gums reveal reduction in carcinogenic microbes

articles.title: Will the mRNA flu shot work better than a regular seasonal one? What the science says
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 13 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02502-8Moderna’s newly approved vaccine could allow manufacturers to respond more rapidly to changing influenza strains.
articles.content:
The number of influenza infections could be reduced by an mRNA vaccine.Credit: Science Photo Library

On 5 August, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval to Moderna’s mRNA-based flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA, for adults aged 50–64, and accelerated approval for adults aged 65 and older. Moderna say it will be available “in a few weeks” to be rolled out for the 2026–27 flu season in the United States.

Researchers welcomed the decision, noting that the vaccine’s mRNA platform allows it to be rapidly reformulated to match circulating influenza strains. “This approval is very important and can be a great game changer” because the platform could help solve the problem of slow manufacturing, says Emanuele Montomoli, a researcher in hygiene and public health at the University of Siena, Italy.

The vaccine is also being reviewed by regulatory agencies in the European Union, Canada and Australia. A related product has already been permitted for use in Europe: in April, the European Commission approved Moderna’s combined seasonal influenza and COVID-19 mRNA vaccine mCombriax.

Tests on more than 40,000 adults showed that 2% of people who received the mFLUSIVA vaccine (called mRNA-1010 before FDA approval) developed a laboratory-confirmed case of flu, verified through testing and symptoms reports1. By comparison, 2.8% of those who received a standard dose of a comparator non-mRNA vaccine developed symptoms.

The tangled history of mRNA vaccines

“The key questions regarding immunogenicity, efficacy and safety have been addressed, which enabled the licensure of mFLUSIVA,” said Raffael Nachbagauer, vice-president of infectious-disease research at Moderna in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who is involved in mFLUSIVA trials.

But scientists still have questions about how this vaccine will perform when it’s rolled out to millions of people. Moderna has agreed with the FDA to conduct a confirmatory phase IV trial to research the efficacy relative to an enhanced vaccine in people aged 65 and older, says Nachbagauer.

Better flu immunity?

The mFLUSIVA vaccine works by delivering mRNA molecules encoding the flu virus’s hemagglutinin surface protein, packaged in a lipid nanoparticle that carries it into cells. Cells then translate the mRNA into hemagglutinin protein, which the immune system recognizes and subsequently builds antibodies against.

Clinical studies evaluating the efficacy of mFLUSIVA found that it had a 26.6% relative reduction in confirmed flu cases compared with a standard influenza vaccine. The investigation tested antigens from the three 2024–25 strains that were recommended by the World Health Organization in time for the corresponding Northern Hemisphere influenza season.

The study also found that mFLUSIVA was well tolerated by most participants. Adverse side effects were predominantly mild to moderate, with injection-site pain, fatigue and headache the most frequently reported. Side effects were more common in people who received the mRNA vaccine versus a standard dose vaccine — for example, injection-site pain was reported more than twice as often with mFLUSIVA as with the standard-dose comparator.

The ghost of influenza past and the hunt for a universal vaccine

A separate study2 in people over the age of 65 comparing mFLUSIVA with licensed comparators contributed to mFLUSIVA’s accelerated approval in the 65-and-older age group. It measured participants’ antibody responses to flu rather than flu-like symptoms, and found that a single dose of the mRNA flu vaccine produced a stronger antibody response than did existing standard-dose and high-dose flu shots.

“A relative improvement over a standard-dose influenza vaccine is already clinically meaningful,” says Federico Martinón-Torres, head of paediatrics at the University Clinical Hospital of Santiago de Compostela, Spain.

articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year, flu vaccines are updated to protect against the most common flu strains. But traditional flu vaccines can take a long time to make and might not always match the flu viruses people catch.

**What happened** – On August 5, 2026, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Moderna’s new mRNA flu vaccine called mFLUSIVA for adults aged 50 to 64, with faster approval for those 65 and older. This vaccine will be available for the 2026–27 flu season in the United States. It uses mRNA technology, the same approach used in some COVID-19 vaccines, to help the body build protection against the flu.

**Impact** – Clinical tests with over 40,000 adults showed that mFLUSIVA reduced flu cases by about 27% compared to regular flu vaccines. It also produced stronger immune responses, especially in older adults. Unlike traditional vaccines, mRNA vaccines can be quickly updated to match new flu strains, which could help make flu shots more effective each year. While some side effects like sore arms and tiredness were more common, they were mostly mild.

**What’s next step** – Moderna will continue studies to compare this mRNA flu vaccine with other enhanced flu vaccines, especially in people over 65. Regulatory agencies in Europe, Canada, and Australia are also reviewing the vaccine. If successful, this could change how flu vaccines are made and given worldwide.

articles.title: The physical effects of heavy phone use (aka tech neck) and how to address them
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Cervical spine surgeon K. Daniel Riew at Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center has started seeing patients in their 20s. That age group rarely appeared in his practice before. Americans now average about seven hours a day on screens, according to DataReportal, and the physical body adapts […]
The post The physical effects of heavy phone use (aka tech neck) and how to address them first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Cervical spine surgeon K. Daniel Riew at Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center has started seeing patients in their 20s. That age group rarely appeared in his practice before. Americans now average about seven hours a day on screens, according to DataReportal, and the physical body adapts to patterns that repeat.

A spine surgeon, a vision scientist, and a medical sociologist each described what that adaptation looks like. The findings are more specific than the general worry about screen time allows for, and several of them are at odds with standard advice.

What tech neck does to the spine

When the head tilts forward to look at a screen, the muscles at the back of the neck engage to hold it up. Ordinary soreness is the initial result. What matters more is what happens to the cervical discs under sustained, repeated load over years: premature cell death and accelerated degeneration. “Once enough cells have died, there is no going back,” Riew says.

Phones are harder on the neck than other screens because people manage them less deliberately. A monitor can be raised. A phone goes everywhere. Most people holding one at waist or chest height never think about cervical alignment, including those who have already rearranged their work setup because of neck pain.

The conventional advice to sit up straight at 90 degrees is, in Riew’s view, a setup for slouching. He recommends reclining at 25 to 30 degrees with lumbar support and a headrest, which shifts the weight of the head and torso into the chair rather than down through the spine. “I can sit in that position for hours without feeling any pain,” he says.

Why screens probably aren’t causing children’s myopia

Rates of myopia have climbed sharply among children. Screens take the blame by default. Donald Mutti, a vision scientist whose work on the CLEERE study (Collaborative Longitudinal Evaluation of Ethnicity and Refractive Error) shaped the field, thinks that’s probably wrong. Screens may not be raising myopia risk directly. They are, however, keeping children inside, and outdoor time is what the data shows protects against nearsightedness.

A study using smartwatch data supported that picture. Two hours of outdoor time per day delivered the maximum protection against developing myopia. The outdoor time needed to last at least 15 minutes per outing, and the light needed to hit 2,000 lux, roughly four times standard office illumination. Shorter or dimmer exposure did nothing. “2,000 lux is easily obtainable outdoors, even in shade,” Mutti notes.

For adults, he is largely unconcerned. “I don’t think there is much of any effect in adults beyond eyestrain. Moderation in all things is always good advice.”

What the grip strength decline tracks to

Grip strength, a well-established marker of overall muscular health and longevity, has been falling across the general population. Soft, screen-bound hands tend to get the blame.

Johannes Beller, a professor of medical sociology at Medical University Lausitz-Carl Thiem, pushed back on that in a 2019 study published in the peer-reviewed journal SSM. The team traced the decline to cohorts born well before smartphones existed. Whatever is driving it, the phone is not the only answer.

“Grip strength is valuable precisely because it reflects overall strength and health, not because the hands themselves are the target,” Beller says. “Staying active and strong is something almost anyone can act on, at any age.”

**What happened**
A spine surgeon at a New York hospital noticed more patients in their 20s with neck pain from using phones. A vision scientist said that rising nearsightedness in children is more about less outdoor time than screen use. For children, spending at least two hours outside daily helps protect their eyesight. Grip strength reflects overall health, so staying active is important for everyone.

**What's next step**
Doctors and specialists can use this new knowledge to guide people on safer phone use and healthy habits. People might change how they sit or hold devices and encourage more outdoor time for kids. Researchers may study more ways to prevent damage from daily screen use.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Using phones carefully, supporting good posture, and spending time outdoors can help protect our necks, eyes, and overall health as screen time grows.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les experts expliquent comment l'utilisation intensive du téléphone affecte la santé et comment réduire les risques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Un chirurgien de la colonne vertébrale à New York a remarqué plus de patients dans la vingtaine souffrant de douleurs au cou liées à l'utilisation du téléphone. Un spécialiste de la vision a expliqué que la hausse de la myopie chez les enfants vient surtout d’un manque de temps passé dehors, plus que des écrans. Un autre expert a indiqué que la baisse de la force de préhension est une tendance ancienne, pas directement liée aux téléphones.

Ces résultats montrent que la façon dont on tient le téléphone est plus néfaste que pour d'autres écrans, car il est souvent tenu bas et sans bonne posture. Le conseil habituel de s’asseoir droit pourrait en fait favoriser le affaissement ; mieux vaut s’incliner en arrière avec un bon soutien pour réduire la douleur au cou. Pour les enfants, passer au moins deux heures par jour dehors protège la vue. La force de la poignée reflète la santé globale, donc rester actif est important pour tous.

articles.personality_title_es: Expertos explican cómo el uso excesivo del teléfono afecta la salud y cómo reducir los daños
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Cada vez más personas, especialmente jóvenes adultos, pasan muchas horas al día frente a pantallas. Esto ha provocado nuevos problemas de salud que los médicos están viendo con más frecuencia.

**Qué pasó**
Un cirujano de columna en un hospital de Nueva York notó más pacientes de 20 años con dolor de cuello por usar teléfonos. Expertos encontraron que mirar hacia abajo el teléfono mucho tiempo causa tensión en los músculos del cuello y puede dañar los discos de la columna con el tiempo. Un científico de la visión dijo que el aumento de la miopía en niños se debe más a pasar menos tiempo afuera que al uso de pantallas. Otro experto dijo que la disminución de la fuerza de agarre es una tendencia antigua no causada directamente por teléfonos.

**Impacto**
Los hallazgos muestran que la forma en que la gente sostiene el teléfono es más dañina que otras pantallas porque se suele tener bajo y sin buena postura. El consejo común de sentarse derecho puede causar encorvamiento; mejor recostarse con soporte para reducir el dolor de cuello. Para los niños, pasar al menos dos horas afuera al día protege la vista. La fuerza del agarre refleja la salud general, por eso es importante mantenerse activo.

**Próximo paso**
Los médicos y especialistas pueden usar esta información para guiar a las personas a usar el teléfono de forma más segura y adoptar hábitos saludables. La gente podría cambiar cómo se sienta o sostiene los dispositivos y fomentar más tiempo al aire libre para los niños. Los investigadores podrían estudiar más formas de prevenir daños por el uso diario de pantallas.

**Resumen en una frase**
Usar los teléfonos con cuidado, mantener buena postura y pasar tiempo al aire libre ayuda a proteger el cuello, los ojos y la salud general mientras aumenta el tiempo frente a pantallas.
